recall_prompt: Say how you would answer this — name every property it needs, and say how you would check them all on one relation.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Name the three properties
steps.margin_note: First mark. All three properties must be named, and each written out. Two out of three is not an equivalence relation, so a list of two earns nothing.
lines: Let R be a relation on a set A, that is R ⊆ A × A.
R is called an equivalence relation if it has all three of these properties:
(i) reflexive:  (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A
(iii) transitive:  (a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R ⇒ (a, c) ∈ R

recall.must_convey: That an equivalence relation is one that is reflexive, symmetric and transitive, all three together.
accept: reflexive symmetric and transitive all three together
a relation with all three properties is an equivalence relation
name the three and write each condition out
moodu properties unte equivalence relation avuthundi

steps.why: This definition is the three earlier definitions taken together, so writing them as a numbered list shows each one is known separately and will be checked separately.
steps.memory_tip: Three letters in order: R for reflexive, S for symmetric, T for transitive.
common_mistakes: Naming reflexive and symmetric only, and leaving transitive out.
Saying an equivalence relation is one where a = b, which is only one example of one.
Naming the three properties without writing what each one means.

steps.label: Check all three on one example
steps.margin_note: Second mark. One relation, three checks, one line each. A relation that fails any single one of the three is not an equivalence relation, so all three lines must be on the page.
lines: Take A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and let a R b mean a and b leave the same remainder on division by 2.
Symmetric: (1,3) has (3,1) in R, and (2,4) has (4,2) in R.
Transitive: (1,3) with (3,1) gives (1,1) ∈ R, and (3,1) with (1,3) gives (3,3) ∈ R; the same holds for 2 and 4.

lines.text: ∴ R is an equivalence relation on A.

recall.must_convey: That one relation is chosen and all three properties are checked on it in turn.
accept: take same remainder on division by two and check all three properties
check reflexive then symmetric then transitive on the same relation
the odd numbers group together and the even numbers group together
same remainder relation ki moodu properties check cheyyali
one three and three one are both there so it is symmetric

steps.why: Working all three checks on one relation is what separates this question from the three before it: the properties are separate conditions on the same list of pairs, and only holding all three at once makes the relation an equivalence relation.
steps.memory_tip: Relations of the form same remainder or same value are always equivalence relations — a safe example to keep ready.
common_mistakes: Checking reflexive only, because the (a, a) pairs are the easiest to see.
Adding (1, 2) to R, which puts an odd number with an even one and breaks the grouping.
Writing three different relations, one for each property, instead of one relation checked three times.
